cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low / Not applicable for panel follow-up: cross-sectional interview recruitment achieved 27 of 35 invited active committee members (77% participation; 8 non-participants without stated reasons for refusal).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk if interpreted causally (not applicable to descriptive qualitative aims): single-basin case study without a counterfactual comparator basin cannot disentangle epistemic Ways of Knowing from utility political-financial power, historical infrastructure lock-in, and São Paulo state emergency re-centralization.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: accurately situates the Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ) River Basin Committees, Executive Agency, and Technical Chambers within Brazil's 1997 Water Law decentralized IWRM framework and reviews official state and basin master plans (2010–2020, 2016–2019, 2020–2035), but discusses emergency rationing decrees, committee deliberation rules, and statutory mandates descriptively without citing specific statutory provisions or formal administrative instruments.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: triangulates 27 semi-structured interviews with multi-year meeting observations (2014–2016; Oct–Dec 2018) and planning documents, but lacks researcher reflexivity, omits interview duration and audio-recording mechanics, and does not report translation verification or inter-coder agreement procedures in NVivo.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for institutional-governance framing outcomes; Weak for physical water/sanitation outcomes: captures committee planning priorities and actor discourses directly, but relies on stakeholder perceptions and planning agendas rather than objective hydrological, water-supply reliability, rationing, or sanitation coverage metrics.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: presents competing engineering and environmental perspectives with direct quotations, structured synthesis (Table 1), and theme proportions (Figure 2), though the interview guide, document list, and detailed coding summaries are placed in online Supplementary Material and raw transcripts are restricted for confidentiality.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern: snowball sampling from key informants recruited 27 active members across stakeholder groups (14 water users, 5 government, 4 civil society, 4 unaffiliated) out of 600 nominal members, appropriately targeting active deliberators but underrepresenting inactive or resource-constrained voices and omitting reasons for 8 refusals.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The Abstract and Introduction clearly state the study's objective: to examine how technocratic insulation, competing ways of knowing (WoKs), and participatory river basin governance shaped planning decisions in Brazil's Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ) River Basin following the 2014–2015 water crisis and their implications for long-term climate resilience.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1 (Abstract); PDF Page 2 (Introduction, final paragraph)

domain_ratings.justification: Investigating how water managers and river basin committee members interpret drought crises, frame policy problems, exercise epistemic authority, and negotiate competing Ways of Knowing directly requires qualitative inquiry into actor narratives and institutional practices.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–4 (Introduction; Ways of Knowing, Adaptive Management, and Solving Crises); PDF Pages 5–6 (Methods)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: An embedded qualitative institutional case study of the PCJ Committees triangulating official basin/state water plans and news media, longitudinal observation of committee and technical chamber meetings (2014–2016 and October–December 2018), and semi-structured interviews with active committee members is well suited to trace governance dynamics after the 2014–2015 drought.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Noting that only a minority of the 600 nominal PCJ governance members actively attend meetings, the authors used snowball sampling from key informants until saturation (no new names suggested), inviting 35 active members across stakeholder sectors and disciplines and interviewing 27 (14 water users, 5 government, 4 civil society, 4 unaffiliated; 11 engineers and 16 from other disciplines), though reasons for the 8 non-participants are not reported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined semi-structured in-person interviews conducted September–December 2018 (guided by an interview protocol in Supplementary Appendix A, with snowball recruitment continuing until saturation), observation of dozens of committee and technical group meetings (2014–2016; October–December 2018), and systematic review of planning documents and news articles, although exact interview durations and fieldnote recording procedures are not specified.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors note observing dozens of meetings, state their belief that interviewees spoke candidly, and acknowledge an academic colleague for facilitating introductions, they provide no critical reflexivity regarding their own disciplinary positionality, normative commitment to adaptive management, or potential observer/gatekeeper influence on participant framing.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The study obtained review and approval from the University of Michigan Health Sciences and Behavioral Sciences Institutional Review Board (IRB-HSBS), documented waiver of written informed consent in accordance with national and institutional rules, restricted dataset access to protect privacy and confidentiality, and attributed quotes only to generalized institutional roles.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7–8 (Results, anonymized role attributions); PDF Page 11 (Data Availability Statement; Ethics Statement)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While the authors describe transcribing, translating, and coding interviews in NVivo via a two-stage deductive and emergent content analysis (citing Saldaña, 2021) and support claims with multi-perspective quotes, Figure 2, and Table 1, they do not report whether multiple coders independently coded transcripts, how inter-coder discrepancies were resolved, how Portuguese-to-English translations were verified, or how discrepant cases were handled in the main text.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 6 (Methods, paragraph 3); PDF Pages 6–9 (Results, Figure 2, Table 1)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized and contrasted across the dominant engineering/IWRM Way of Knowing and the minority environmental/adaptive Way of Knowing (Table 1, Figure 2), illustrated with verbatim quotations from opposing stakeholder groups, corroborated by meeting observations, and explicitly linked back to the research question.

Substantively valuable contribution to water governance scholarship: demonstrates empirically how epistemic hierarchies and state-utility power asymmetries within formally decentralized, participatory river basin institutions (under Brazil's 1997 Water Law) perpetuate grey-infrastructure lock-in after extreme drought, offering transferable lessons for polycentric and adaptive water governance reforms.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable empirical and conceptual contribution (narrative assessment)

overall_narrative_summary: Almazán-Casali, Peregrina Puga, and Lemos (2021) present a well-contextualized primary qualitative case study examining why Brazil's decentralized, participatory Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ) River Basin Committees doubled down on grey-infrastructure solutions rather than adaptive or nature-based governance after the 2014–2015 São Paulo water crisis. Methodological strengths include clear research aims (Q1), an appropriate qualitative case design triangulating master water plans, news coverage, multi-year observation of committee and technical chamber meetings, and 27 semi-structured interviews across engineering and non-engineering committee actors (Q2–Q5), documented IRB approval and confidentiality protections (Q7), and balanced, transparent presentation of competing Ways of Knowing (Q9–Q10). Moderate methodological concern arises from two gaps out of Q1–Q9: the absence of researcher reflexivity regarding multi-year observer presence, academic gatekeeper introductions, and normative theoretical framing (Q6: No), and incomplete reporting of analytic rigor regarding coder independence/consensus in NVivo and Portuguese-to-English translation verification (Q8: Can't tell). Moreover, snowball recruitment among active committee participants leaves inactive or marginalized stakeholders outside the core deliberative arenas unexamined, and water/sanitation governance effects are assessed through institutional planning priorities and perceptions rather than physical service-delivery outcomes.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 No and 1 Can't tell item out of Q1-Q9)
study_design_identified: Primary qualitative single-basin case study combining semi-structured interviews (n = 27), longitudinal participant observation of river basin committee and technical chamber meetings, and documentary/media content analysis
where_found_summary: Research aims and institutional context on PDF Pages 1–5 (Abstract, Introduction, An Overview of Brazilian Water Governance, Ways of Knowing framework); documentary review, meeting observation (2014–2016; Oct–Dec 2018), snowball recruitment (35 invited, 27 interviewed), and two-stage NVivo coding in Methods on PDF Pages 5–6; thematic findings, Figure 2, Table 1, and stakeholder quotations in Results on PDF Pages 6–9; synthesis and policy implications on PDF Pages 9–11 (Discussion, Conclusions); privacy, IRB-HSBS approval, funding, and gatekeeper acknowledgments on PDF Page 11.
why_tool_chosen: The study's empirical Methods (PDF Pages 5–6) consist entirely of qualitative data collection and thematic content analysis—27 semi-structured interviews with PCJ River Basin Committee members, participant observation of committee meetings, and qualitative review of basin master plans and media coverage. Descriptive theme proportions in Figure 2 merely summarize coded qualitative interview themes rather than constituting a distinct quantitative survey or econometric design, and there is no counterfactual comparator group, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the exact matching appraisal tool.
